newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S., Chinese leaders agree to exchange visits.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Chinese leaders agree to exchange visits.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin opened a new chapter in Sino-U.S. relations on Sunday by agreeing on a framework for summitry over the next two years.

Meeting on the eve of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Clinton and Jiang confirmed a thawing of relations between the United States and China that has been under discussion since U.S. National Security Adviser Anthony Lake visited Beijing in July.

Clinton, on his first foreign tour since his November 5 re-election, also held talks with South Korean President Kim Young-sam and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on the fringes of the APEC conference.
But his meeting with Jiang grabbed the spotlight at the annual trade meeting.

"The two presidents have accepted each other's invitation for state visits. They will make those visits during 1997 and 1998 at a time and (in) a sequence to be determined by their foreign ministers," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters after the 85-minute meeting.

The last U.S. president to visit China was George Bush in 1989. Ties between the United States and China started unravelling in June of that year because of the Tiananmen Square massacre of pro-democracy protesters and have been more or less frosty since.

Clinton and Jiang, holding their fourth meeting in four years, agreed on the importance of regular high-level visits, McCurry said. As part of this process, Vice President Al Gore will visit China "sometime during the first half of 1997", he said.

A senior U.S. official who briefed reporters after the two presidents met indicated they agreed on very little beyond an exchange of summits at their meeting, which the official described as "very straightforward" and "businesslike". Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang described the talks as constructive, and said the presidents agreed their meeting was important for the future of U.S.-China relations.

The U.S. official said Clinton and Jiang covered an array of issues, including nuclear non-proliferation, Taiwan, China's push for membership in the World Trade Organisation (WTO), North Korea and human rights.

North Korea was also the focus of Clinton's meeting with Kim, at which they called on Pyongyang to take unspecified "acceptable steps" to reduce tensions on the Korean peninsula arising from the recent bloody aftermath of a North Korean submarine grounding in South Korean coastal waters.
Several South Korean troops and civilians were killed during a manhunt for crewmembers who fled the scene of apparent infiltration.

Clinton rejected Jiang's call for an end to U.S. sponsorship of a U.N. resolution that criticises China's record on human rights, and also told him that China needs to do more to become a member of the WTO trade body, the official said.
He said Jiang complained about U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, but that this was not a major topic of discussion.

Despite their differences, the Clinton-Jiang meeting was apparently cordial and had some light-hearted moments. When Clinton noted that he was hoarse because of his recent re-election campaign and the rigours of his current trip, Jiang jokingly urged him to try Chinese acupuncture.

The Chinese leader also told Clinton that the wreck of a U.S. B-24 bomber had recently been found in southern China with some human remains aboard, apparently those of U.S. servicemen missing since World War Two.
Jiang gave the U.S. president a videotape and photographs of the crash site and invited him to send a U.S. forensic team to China to inspect it.

Clinton sandwiched a 45-minute meeting with Hashimoto between talks with Jiang and Kim, and the White House called the session constructive. Hashimoto welcomed the thaw in Sino-U.S. relations, a senior Japanese government official said.
Asked by reporters if he and the prime minister had made progress on trade issues, Clinton said Hashimoto had "reaffirmed his willingness to resolve any remaining disputes between us".

"If the economy keeps growing in Japan, that should help us reduce the trade imbalance," Clinton said. A Japanese official said Clinton also stressed the need for progress on a thorny bilateral dispute over Japan's insurance market.
